title: BST iterator
statement:
$7a

**Example 1:**

```
Input : [ "BSTIterator" , "next" , "next" , "hasNext" , "next" , "hasNext" , "next" , "hasNext" , "next" , "hasNext" ] , root = [7, 3, 15, null, null, 9, 20]
Output : [3, 7, true, 9, true, 15, true, 20, false]
Explanation :
BSTIterator bSTIterator = new BSTIterator([7, 3, 15, null, null, 9, 20]);
bSTIterator.next(); // return 3
bSTIterator.next(); // return 7
bSTIterator.hasNext(); // return True
bSTIterator.next(); // return 9
bSTIterator.hasNext(); // return True
bSTIterator.next(); // return 15
bSTIterator.hasNext(); // return True
bSTIterator.next(); // return 20
bSTIterator.hasNext(); // return False
```

**Example 2:**

```
Input : [ "BSTIterator" , "next" , "next" , "next", "hasNext" , "next" , "hasNext" ] , root = [7, 3, 15, null, null, 9, 20]
Output : [3, 7, 9, true, 15, true]
Explanation :
BSTIterator bSTIterator = new BSTIterator([7, 3, 15, null, null, 9, 20]);
bSTIterator.next(); // return 3
bSTIterator.next(); // return 7
bSTIterator.next(); // return 9
bSTIterator.hasNext(); // return True
bSTIterator.next(); // return 15
bSTIterator.hasNext(); // return True
```
constraints:
- 1 <= Number of Nodes <= 104
- At most 104 calls will be made to next and hasNext.
- 0 <= Node.val <= 1054

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.body: "Perform an inorder traversal during initialization and store the elements in an array. next() simply returns the next element from the stored list. hasNext() checks if more elements are available."

hints.title: Hint 2
hints.body: "Instead of storing all elements, use a stack to simulate recursion. Push all left children first. When next() is called: Pop the top element. Push its right subtree’s leftmost path into the stack."

doubts.question: Why do we use a stack instead of storing the entire inorder traversal?
doubts.answer:
Optimizes space from O(n) to O(h), where h is the tree height.
Ensures O(1) average time complexity for next().

doubts.question: Why do we push only left children initially?
doubts.answer: Inorder traversal = Left → Root → Right, so we process leftmost nodes first.

followUps.question: How would you modify this iterator to support prev() for reverse traversal?
followUps.answer: Use two stacks (one for normal and one for reversed inorder).

followUps.question: Can this iterator be extended to work on general binary trees?
followUps.answer: Yes, but inorder traversal would not guarantee sorted order.

facts: Database engines use ordered indexes to expose records through cursor-like iterators, returning keys in sorted order without loading the entire result set at once.
Lazy ordered traversal is useful in schedulers and event systems when the next smallest timestamp is needed incrementally rather than all events upfront.
